$$
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i = 7.
$$

Find the likelihood function of the sample.

*Hint: The probability mass function for a Bernoulli random variable is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\theta^x (1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x = 0,1.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability mass function is

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0,1.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}} \\  & =({\theta }^{{x}_{1}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{1}})\cdot ({\theta }^{{x}_{2}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{2}})\,⋯\,({\theta }^{{x}_{n}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{n}}) \\  & ={\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,\sum (1-{x}_{i})} \\  & ={\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,n-\sum {x}_{i}} \\  & ={\theta }^{S}(1-\theta )^{n-S}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i.$ 

We are told that $\displaystyle S=\sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i=7$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\theta }^{7}(1-\theta )^{10-7} \\  & ={\theta }^{7}(1-\theta )^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176062 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-43e2161d-2ae7-5d04-bc29-2934b939fe8c" "question-cec4340f-d49e-5a8e-a40d-7d35274dd0d2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175708 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{12}$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim B(4,\theta)$ and unknown probability of success $\theta.$ For a particular sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{12},$ you're given that 

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{12} x_i = 22.
$$

Find the likelihood function of the sample up to a constant $C.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x) = \displaystyle \binom{n}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{n-x}, \qquad x = 0,1,2,\ldots, n.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 12$ independent binomial random variables with unknown probability of success $\theta$ and $N = 4$ trials, for which the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x;\theta )=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x}, & \,x=0,1,2,3,4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta ) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}} \\  & =((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{1}}){\theta }^{{x}_{1}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{1}})\cdot ((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{2}}){\theta }^{{x}_{2}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{2}})⋯((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{n}}){\theta }^{{x}_{n}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{n}}) \\  & =C\,{\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,\sum (4-{x}_{i})} \\  & =C\,{\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,4n-\sum {x}_{i}} \\  & =C\,{\theta }^{S}(1-\theta )^{4n-S}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle C = \prod\limits_{i=1}^n  {4 \choose x_i}$ is a constant and $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^{n} x_i.$

We are told that $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^{n} x_i = 22$ and $n = 12.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =C\,{\theta }^{22}(1-\theta )^{4(12)-22} \\  & =C\,{\theta }^{22}(1-\theta )^{26}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176063 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-83f5b615-5500-5815-8837-5144deae0691"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175709 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \mathrm{Po}(\theta)$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ Find the likelihood function of the sample $0, 2, 3, 1, 1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta,$ for which the probability mass function is

$$
f(x; \theta) = \dfrac{\theta^{x} e^{-\theta}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots\,.
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta ) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{i}!} \\  & =(\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{1}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{1}!})\cdot (\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{2}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{2}!})⋯(\frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{n}}{e}^{-\theta }}{{x}_{n}!}) \\  & ={\theta }^{\sum {x}_{i}}\cdot {e}^{-\sum \theta }\cdot {\prod }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{({x}_{i})!} \\  & ={\theta }^{\sum {x}_{i}}\cdot {e}^{-n\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i})!} \\  & =\frac{1}{C}\,{\theta }^{S}\,{e}^{-n\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle C=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n} (x_i)!$ is a constant and $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0+2+3+1+1 \\  & =7 \\ C & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i})! \\  & =0!\cdot 2!\cdot 3!\cdot 1!\cdot 1! \\  & =1\cdot 2\cdot 6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

 

and $n=5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{12}\,{\theta }^{7}\,{e}^{-5\theta }.\end{aligned}

We wish to develop strategies to estimate unknown population parameters from sample data. One such strategy is to use **likelihood functions.** 

In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute likelihood functions for particular discrete probability distributions.

Suppose we have an I.I.D. (independent and identically distributed) random sample

$$
X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_n,
$$

where the probability mass function of each $X_i$ is given by

$$
f(x;\,\theta)
$$

and $\theta$ is an *unknown,* fixed parameter. 

Suppose we have a particular sample from this distribution:

$$
x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n
$$

We define the **likelihood function** $L(\theta)$ as 

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n).
$$

The likelihood function gives the probability of getting a particular sample for a specific parameter value. 

Now, since we assumed that all $X_i$'s are independent and identically distributed, by the multiplication law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1})\cdot P({X}_{2}={x}_{2})⋯P({X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}P({X}_{i}={x}_{i}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, the likelihood function $L(\theta)$ is defined as

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177074 :tutorial/content "Suppose that 

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3,\quad X_4,\quad X_5,\quad X_6
$$

 

is an I.I.D random sample from a population, where 

$$
X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta)
$$

and $\theta$ is the *unknown* probability of success. 

Suppose we conduct a sample and get the following data:

$$
x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1
$$

 

Let's compute the likelihood function for this sample.

Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are I.I.D random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

The probability mass function for a Bernoulli random variable with an unknown probability of success $\theta$ is given by

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0,1.
$$

Using this definition, we can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}} \\  & =({\theta }^{{x}_{1}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{1}})\cdot ({\theta }^{{x}_{2}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{2}})\,⋯\,({\theta }^{{x}_{n}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{n}}) \\  & ={\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,\sum (1-{x}_{i})} \\  & ={\theta }^{\,\sum {x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{\,n-\sum {x}_{i}} \\  & ={\theta }^{S}(1-\theta )^{n-S}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i.$ 

For our sample, we have that $n=6,$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0+1+1+0+1+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the likelihood function for this sample is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\theta }^{4}(1-\theta )^{6-4} \\  & ={\theta }^{4}(1-\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of $L(\theta)$ is shown below. 

![](images/28/28c73749a566d5531ef2f13c5b01bd1d26ced28e19749abf056841492fb497f5.png)

Notice that $L(\theta)$ has a maximum inside the interval $\theta \in [0,1].$ The value $\widehat{\,\theta\,}$ that corresponds to the maximum likelihood is called the **maximum likelihood estimate** of the parameter $\theta$ for the given sample. 

We'll discuss how to compute the maximum likelihood estimate in future topics. But, for now, let's see more examples of finding the likelihood functions for different distributions and samples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176143 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

We wish to develop strategies to estimate unknown population parameters from sample data. One such strategy is to use **likelihood functions.** 

In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute likelihood functions for particular discrete probability distributions.

Suppose we have an I.I.D. (independent and identically distributed) random sample

$$
X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_n,
$$

where the probability mass function of each $X_i$ is given by

$$
f(x;\,\theta)
$$

and $\theta$ is an *unknown,* fixed parameter. 

Suppose we have a particular sample from this distribution:

$$
x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n
$$

We define the **likelihood function** $L(\theta)$ as 

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n).
$$

The likelihood function gives the probability of getting a particular sample for a specific parameter value. 

Now, since we assumed that all $X_i$'s are independent and identically distributed, by the multiplication law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1})\cdot P({X}_{2}={x}_{2})⋯P({X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}P({X}_{i}={x}_{i}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, the likelihood function $L(\theta)$ is defined as

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

We wish to develop strategies to estimate unknown population parameters from sample data. One such strategy is to use **likelihood functions.** 

In this lesson, we'll learn how to compute likelihood functions for particular discrete probability distributions.

Suppose we have an I.I.D. (independent and identically distributed) random sample

$$
X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_n,
$$

where the probability mass function of each $X_i$ is given by

$$
f(x;\,\theta)
$$

and $\theta$ is an *unknown,* fixed parameter. 

Suppose we have a particular sample from this distribution:

$$
x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n
$$

We define the **likelihood function** $L(\theta)$ as 

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n).
$$

The likelihood function gives the probability of getting a particular sample for a specific parameter value. 

Now, since we assumed that all $X_i$'s are independent and identically distributed, by the multiplication law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & =P({X}_{1}={x}_{1})\cdot P({X}_{2}={x}_{2})⋯P({X}_{n}={x}_{n}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}P({X}_{i}={x}_{i}) \\  & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, the likelihood function $L(\theta)$ is defined as

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

$$

$$

$$

Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are I.I.D random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta)$, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0,1

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= θ^{S}(1 - θ)^{n - S}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{6 - 4} \\
&= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1
$$

Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are I.I.D random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta)$, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

The probability mass function for a Bernoulli random variable with an unknown probability of success $\theta$ is given by

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0,1
$$

Using this definition, we can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i} \\
&= θ) \\
&= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)θ^{x_{i}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{i}} \\
&= (θ^{x_{1}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{1}}) \cdot (θ^{x_{2}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{2}})⋯(θ^{x_{n}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{n}}) \\

&= θ^{∑x_{i}}(1 - θ)^{n - ∑x_{i}} \\
&= θ^{S}(1 - θ)^{n - S}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i
$$

For our sample, we have that $n=6$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the likelihood function for this sample is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{6 - 4} \\
&= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/28/28c73749a566d5531ef2f13c5b01bd1d26ced28e19749abf056841492fb497f5.png)

Using this definition, we can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i} \\
&= θ) \\
&= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)θ^{x_{i}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{i}} \\
&= (θ^{x_{1}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{1}}) \cdot (θ^{x_{2}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{2}})⋯(θ^{x_{n}}(1 - θ)^{1 - x_{n}}) \\
&= θ^{∑x_{i}}(1 - θ)^{∑(1 - x_{i})} \\
&= θ^{∑x_{i}}(1 - θ)^{n - ∑x_{i}} \\
&= θ^{S}(1 - θ)^{n - S}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\displaystyle S = \sum\limits_ {i=1}^n x_i
$$

For our sample, we have that $n=6$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} \\
&= 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the likelihood function for this sample is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(θ) &= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{6 - 4} \\
&= θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

&= ∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i} \\
